You are a rigorous speculative world-builder working for a film production. You
extrapolate societies forward two years at a time from a documented starting
state and a set of drivers that are stipulated as having come true. You are not
writing a thriller. You are writing the minutes of a world. Every change you
describe must have a visible mechanism; magnitudes must be defensible for a
two-year window; nothing happens because it is dramatic. Where the drivers pull
against each other, you show the friction rather than resolving it.

You write for an audience that includes an endocrinologist, a health economist,
a food-industry analyst and a political reporter. Any one of them should finish
your world and say "I don't like it, but I can't dismiss it."

You are a rigorous speculative world-builder working for a film production. You
extrapolate societies forward two years at a time from a documented starting
state and a set of drivers that are stipulated as having come true. You are not
writing a thriller. You are writing the minutes of a world. Every change you
describe must have a visible mechanism; magnitudes must be defensible for a
two-year window; nothing happens because it is dramatic. Where the drivers pull
against each other, you show the friction rather than resolving it.

You write for an audience that includes an endocrinologist, a health economist,
a food-industry analyst and a political reporter. Any one of them should finish
your world and say "I don't like it, but I can't dismiss it."

That is almost exactly the number two years ago, and the flatness hides a great deal of movement. New users keep arriving, drawn by a retatrutide that now costs $299 a month and takes off nearly a third of body weight. Others leave just as steadily: a job changes, an employer narrows its formulary, a Medicare beneficiary misses too many refills and is locked out for a year, or a cash buyer reads about the counterfeit pens and stops. Nearly 24 million adults have been on the drug and are off it now. A third of everyone who has ever used it has stopped and started again at least once.\n\nThe structure of who pays has not changed. If a person has diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea or a fatty liver, insurance still pays. If they have only obesity, it probably doesn't: 43 percent of employers cover weight management, down one point. Medicare still pays $245 under the Continuity Model and still checks refills. The middle class still buys brand product through TrumpRx, where the pills start at $149 and injectable semaglutide has slipped to $179. Washington passed no new law and launched no new programme. The FDA issued warnings, Congress held hearings, and nothing else happened. The gray market lost a million users to fear and gained them back on price. Lilly and Novo now ship pens with serial numbers that a phone can verify, and two wellness vendors already read those scans as proof of adherence.\n\nThe label brought alcohol. In June semaglutide was approved for alcohol use disorder, with no weight requirement, the first time the drug has been sold to people who are not heavy. Addiction clinics began prescribing within weeks. Spirits makers, already down for four years, wrote that analysts expected a faster decline. The telehealth firms had arrived earlier. Since autumn 2029 they have sold 'Quiet Mind', low-dose pills for food noise and mental chatter, to 400,000 subscribers. No regulator has objected, and no trial has measured what quieter wanting costs. The FDA asked doctors to measure growth, and pediatric starts fell. Nobody yet knows about adult height, and the answer will come after US generics arrive.\n\nIn the suburbs of Plano, Columbus and Phoenix, being on the drug has stopped being news. A mid-life body that hasn't changed draws a gentle question: have you tried it, or is it coverage? Caterers plan for light plates and dating apps carry an 'on it' field. The Zepbound itself she pays for, $279 on the Lilly site, because Ridgeline Logistics covers it only for diabetics.\n\nAt seven she's on the dock outside Columbus, counting pallets. At lunch the break room splits the way it always does now: half the shift eating half a sandwich, half eating the whole one. He threw the box out and hasn't said anything since.\n\nAfter work she takes Kayla, fourteen, to the pediatrician. Kayla has been on Wegovy for a year. The nurse measures her against the wall twice, then once more, and writes something down. The doctor says the word \"velocity\" and that they'll check again in three months. Kayla asks if she has to stop. The doctor says it's a conversation.\n\nAt home Dale has the grill going. He offers her a beer out of habit and she shakes her head, also out of habit.
